name: Glycerin
lead: Glycerin (glycerol) is a colorless, odorless, sweet-tasting, viscous sugar alcohol that is miscible with water and hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture.[1] It is one of the most common ingredients in skin care, hair care, soaps, shaving products and personal lubricants, where it functions as a humectant and gives a smooth feel.[1]

Beyond cosmetics it is widely used in medicine and food: as a laxative in suppositories, as an excipient in tablets and syrups, and as the food additive E422.[1] The sources reviewed for this article contain no randomized trial of glycerin as a cosmetic moisturizer, so its skin effects here rest on encyclopedic descriptions and use history rather than on trial data.

paras: Glycerin is used as a humectant and lubricant in skin care, hair care, shaving cream and soaps, and topical glycerin has been used for ichthyosis and xerosis (dry skin).[1] It appears on the WHO Essential Medicines List in the context of atopic eczema.[1]

Rectal glycerin acts as a laxative, oral glycerin has been used to temporarily lower eye pressure in emergencies, and it is used to preserve red blood cells before freezing and to preserve tissue grafts.[1] It is a common solvent in oral and injectable drug formulations.[2] In vaping liquids, vegetable glycerin is a common solvent, and studies have examined the carbonyl compounds produced when it is heated.[3]

Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered glycerin as the sweet principle of fat; Michel Eugène Chevreul coined the name glycérine around 1811, and the alcohol-style name glycerol was introduced in 1872.[1] During World War II, synthetic production from propylene was prioritized because glycerol is a precursor to nitroglycerin, and biofuel production since around 2010 has created a surplus.[1]

Wikipedia reports very low oral toxicity in animal tests, though excessive intake by children, for example through glycerol-containing slush drinks, can cause symptoms such as hypoglycemia, nausea and loss of consciousness; UK and Scottish food authorities issued guidance in 2023.[1] Contamination of glycerol with diethylene glycol has caused deaths in the past, and the FDA advised batch testing in 2007.[1]

No studies found on glycerin as a cosmetic or appearance product in the sources reviewed. Registered trials of glycerin concern other uses, such as suppositories for feeding intolerance in premature infants and for bowel function in gastroschisis.[4][5] A registered study of a cosmetic active ingredient for atopic dermatitis exists but does not identify glycerin as the active.[6]

timeline.event: The name glycerol, with the alcohol suffix, is introduced.[1]
FDA advises testing glycerol batches for diethylene glycol contamination.[1]

card.summary: The ubiquitous humectant in moisturizers and cleansers, with long use but no cosmetic trials in the sources reviewed.
card.note: Evidence for skin effects here is descriptive; diethylene glycol contamination has been a historical safety issue.

quick.overview:
Glycerin is a thick, sweet, water-attracting liquid that appears in most moisturizers, soaps and many hair and shaving products. It is also used as a laxative, drug excipient and food additive.

The sources reviewed describe its role as a humectant but contain no cosmetic trials; the registered trials found study other uses such as suppositories.
quick.mechanism: It is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water, which is why it is described as a humectant that softens skin.
quick.risks: Oral toxicity is described as very low, but large amounts can affect children, and past diethylene glycol contamination caused deaths, leading to FDA batch-testing advice in 2007.
